title: Fractions, Decimals & Percents
coreInsight: Fractions, decimals, and percents are different representations of the same quantities, and a fraction is itself a number with a location and magnitude.
targetLearnerRealization: Fractions, decimals, and percents can name the same location on a number line and should be compared by magnitude rather than by separate digit rules.
learningObjectives: Interpret a fraction as one number located on a number line.
Connect fraction, decimal, and percent names for the same magnitude.
Compare fractions and decimals using benchmarks and structure.
Interpret a percent relative to a specified whole.

continuity.openingCallback: Use the unmarked positions between whole numbers to create and name a new magnitude.
closingSeeds: A fraction compares a selected amount with a whole.
Two quantities can also be compared directly and scaled together.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: The numerator and denominator behave like two independent whole numbers.
A larger denominator automatically means a larger fraction.
More decimal digits automatically means a larger number.
A percent has meaning without identifying the whole it is a percent of.

beats.purpose: Turn an unnamed position inside a whole-number gap into a single fractional quantity.
beats.expectedRealization: Three eighths names one magnitude, not two unrelated whole numbers.
beats.transitionIn: The number line continued inside every whole-number gap. Cut one whole into eight equal lengths and take three of them.
beats.prompt: Which number names the filled length of this one whole?

bars.label: One whole cut into 8 equal parts

visual.ariaLabel: A bar divided into eight equal parts with three filled

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. The denominator records eight equal parts in the whole; the numerator counts the three selected parts.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Read the lower number as the number of equal parts in one whole, and the upper number as how many are selected.

steps.title: Build the unit
steps.body: Dividing one whole into 8 equal parts makes each part 1/8.

steps.title: Count the length
steps.body: Three such parts make 3 × 1/8 = 3/8. Together they form one number between 0 and 1.

resolution.takeaway: A fraction names a magnitude built from equal parts of a whole.

beats.purpose: Unify fraction, decimal, and percent labels at a familiar benchmark before a nontrivial case.
beats.expectedRealization: Different symbols can name the same point.
beats.transitionIn: Change the partition, but keep looking for one location rather than three separate rules.
beats.prompt: A point is halfway from 0 to 1. Select every label that names that same point.

visual.ariaLabel: A number line from zero to one with a tick halfway between

response.feedback: Ask what share of the trip from 0 to 1 each label describes.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. One half, five tenths, and fifty hundredths all land at the same point.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Rewrite each label as a share of one whole: halves, tenths, or hundredths.

visual.ariaLabel: Two equal-length half-filled bars partitioned into halves and tenths

steps.body: 1/2 = 5/10 = 50/100. Decimal notation records five tenths as 0.5; percent notation records fifty hundredths as 50%.

resolution.takeaway: Equivalent forms are different names for one magnitude.

beats.purpose: Extend equivalence to the required nontrivial value 3/8 = 0.375 = 37.5%.
beats.expectedRealization: Division and percent scaling preserve the same underlying magnitude.
beats.transitionIn: Return to the three shaded eighths and give that same length decimal and percent names.
beats.prompt: Which row gives three equivalent names for the filled bar?

visual.ariaLabel: The same bar divided into eight equal parts with three filled

beats.correctFeedback: Right. Dividing 3 by 8 gives 0.375, which is 37.5 hundredths.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Compute 3 ÷ 8, then multiply that decimal by 100 to count hundredths of the whole.

beats.purpose: Repair the belief that a larger denominator makes a larger fraction.
beats.expectedRealization: With the same numerator, more equal cuts make each selected piece smaller.
beats.transitionIn: Equivalent names preserve a length. Now keep the number of selected pieces fixed while changing their size.
beats.prompt: Both bars select three pieces from one equal-length whole. Which fraction is larger?

visual.ariaLabel: Equal-length bars showing three fourths and three eighths

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Fourths are larger pieces than eighths, so three fourths is longer.
beats.incorrectFeedback: The wholes have equal length. Compare the size of one fourth with one eighth.

steps.body: Cutting a fixed whole into more equal pieces makes each piece smaller. With three pieces selected in both bars, 3/8 < 3/4.

resolution.takeaway: A larger denominator means smaller pieces when the whole is fixed.

beats.purpose: Repair digit-count comparison by returning decimals to magnitude.
beats.expectedRealization: Decimal length does not determine decimal size.
beats.transitionIn: Piece counts can mislead. Digit counts can mislead in the same way.

options.text: They are equal because both are less than 1.

beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Writing 0.8 as 0.800 aligns the place values, and 800 thousandths exceeds 375 thousandths.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Add trailing zeros without changing value: compare 0.800 with 0.375.

resolution.takeaway: Compare place values, not the number of written digits.

beats.purpose: Make the reference whole essential to interpreting a percent.
beats.expectedRealization: The same percent can represent different amounts when the wholes differ.
beats.transitionIn: A percent names a share of a whole. Change the whole and watch the amount change.
beats.prompt: One box holds 20 beads and another holds 200 beads. Is 50% of each box the same number of beads?

options.text: Yes; the percent symbol fixes the amount.
No; the amounts are 10 beads and 100 beads.
No; the amounts are 20 beads and 200 beads.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. Half of 20 is 10, while half of 200 is 100.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Translate 50% to one half, then take one half of each stated whole.

steps.body: 50% describes the same proportion—one half—in both boxes. The wholes differ, so the resulting bead counts differ: 10 and 100.

resolution.takeaway: Always identify the whole behind a percent.

beats.purpose: Name the three representations after their shared magnitudes have been experienced.
beats.expectedRealization: Notation changes while the underlying number stays fixed.
beats.transitionIn: Bars, place value, and parts of a whole all point to one idea.
beats.name: Equivalent fraction, decimal, and percent forms
beats.conciseDefinition: A fraction describes equal parts or division, a decimal records place value, and a percent counts hundredths. Equivalent forms name the same number.
beats.memoryHook: Change the name, not the point.

beats.purpose: Apply magnitude structure to order unfamiliar fractions without defaulting to a common-denominator algorithm.
beats.expectedRealization: Shared whole parts and numerators reduce the comparison to slice size.
beats.transitionIn: The bars showed that equal numerators reverse the denominator comparison. These three contest fractions hide that same structure above 1.
beats.whyNow: Once representations are unified by magnitude, ordering several fractions tests whether the learner compares quantities rather than separate digits.
beats.entryBridge: Split each fraction into one whole plus its leftover part before comparing.
beats.exitBridge: The symbols differed, but their shared structure placed all three on one magnitude line.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Equal-length partition bars and the lesson number line.
learnerPrompts: At the first step, rewrite each fraction as 1 plus a leftover fraction.
When the whole bars move aside, what numerator do all three leftovers share?
As the slice lines appear, which denominator makes four pieces thinnest?
On the final number line, read the order from left to right.
beats.correctFeedback: Yes. The common whole and numerator leave slice size to decide: 4/15 < 4/13 < 4/11.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Rewrite each value as 1 plus four equal pieces, then compare how wide those pieces are.

steps.title: Compare equal piece counts
steps.body: All leftovers contain four pieces. Fifteenths are thinnest, then thirteenths, then elevenths, so 4/15 < 4/13 < 4/11.

steps.title: Restore the whole
steps.body: Adding the same 1 preserves the order: 19/15 < 17/13 < 15/11. Therefore the answer is E.

resolution.takeaway: Look for shared structure before reaching for a general algorithm.

beats.purpose: Consolidate representation equivalence and magnitude-based comparison.
beats.expectedRealization: Representations are interchangeable only when they preserve the same whole and location.
beats.transitionIn: The same magnitude survived bars, division, decimals, percents, and an ordering problem.
beats.prompt: Select every statement that is always true.

options.text: Equivalent fraction, decimal, and percent forms name the same point.
A decimal with more written digits is always larger.
The amount represented by a percent depends on the chosen whole.
For a fixed whole and numerator, more denominator pieces make each piece smaller.
A fraction is just two unrelated whole numbers.

response.feedback: Test each claim against the bars for 3/8, the decimals 0.8 and 0.375, and the two bead boxes.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. Compare underlying magnitudes and keep the reference whole visible.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Discard rules based only on digit count or on treating the numerator and denominator separately.

steps.title: Locate
steps.body: Equivalent forms land at one number-line point.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body: Benchmarks, equal partitions, and aligned place values expose magnitude.

steps.title: Interpret
steps.body: A percent describes a share only after its whole is identified.

beats.purpose: Create the forward need to compare two quantities directly rather than only a part with its whole.
beats.expectedRealization: A part-whole fraction does not by itself express every useful comparison in a mixture.
beats.transitionIn: A fraction compared the selected part with one whole. A mixture invites another comparison.
beats.prompt: A bag contains 3 red counters and 5 blue counters. Besides comparing red counters with all 8 counters, what direct comparison might matter?

options.text: Red counters compared with blue counters: 3 to 5.
The number 3 compared with itself only.
The total without referring to either color.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Comparing red directly with blue creates a 3-to-5 relationship.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Look for a comparison that uses both color counts without first combining them.

steps.body: The fraction 3/8 compares red counters with the whole bag. The comparison 3 to 5 relates red counters directly to blue counters. Next we will ask what remains unchanged when both counts scale.

resolution.takeaway: Quantities can be compared part-to-whole or directly to each other.

notes: The linked segmented bars and number-line prompts unify representations before conversion language is named.
